claim: In the rodent olfactory bulb, the smooth dendrites of the principal glutamatergic mitral cells form reciprocal dendrodendritic synapses with large spines on GABAergic granule cells.
source: In the rodent olfactory bulb the smooth dendrites of the principal glutamatergic mitral cells (MCs) form reciprocal dendrodendritic synapses with large spines on GABAergic granule cells (GC)
evidence: This is a well-established anatomical fact about olfactory bulb circuitry, supported by the manuscript's introduction and cited literature.

claim: Unitary release of glutamate can trigger postsynaptic local activation of voltage-gated Na+-channels (spine spike) in granule cell spines.
source: where unitary release of glutamate can trigger postsynaptic local activation of voltage-gated Na+-channels (Navs), that is a spine spike
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by previous work cited in the manuscript (Bywalez et al., 2015).

claim: Unitary-like activation via two-photon uncaging of glutamate causes GC spines to release GABA both synchronously and asynchronously onto MC dendrites.
source: We find that unitary-like activation via two-photon uncaging of glutamate causes GC spines to release GABA both synchronously and asynchronously onto MC dendrites.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and throughout the Results section.

claim: GABA release from GC spines requires activation of voltage-gated Na+-channels.
source: This release indeed requires activation of Navs and high-voltage-activated Ca2+-channels (HVACCs), but also of NMDA receptors (NMDAR).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally through TTX blockade experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: GABA release from GC spines requires activation of high-voltage-activated Ca2+-channels.
source: This release indeed requires activation of Navs and high-voltage-activated Ca2+-channels (HVACCs), but also of NMDA receptors (NMDAR).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally through CTX blockade experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: GABA release from GC spines requires activation of NMDA receptors.
source: This release indeed requires activation of Navs and high-voltage-activated Ca2+-channels (HVACCs), but also of NMDA receptors (NMDAR).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally through APV blockade experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Simulations show temporally overlapping HVACC- and NMDAR-mediated Ca2+-currents during the spine spike.
source: Simulations show temporally overlapping HVACC- and NMDAR-mediated Ca2+-currents during the spine spike
evidence: This is demonstrated through computational modeling shown in Figure 5.

claim: Ultrastructural data prove NMDAR presence within the GABAergic presynapse.
source: ultrastructural data prove NMDAR presence within the GABAergic presynapse
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunogold electron microscopy shown in Figure 6.

claim: Reciprocal dendrodendritic microcircuits are especially abundant in the vertebrate olfactory bulb.
source: Reciprocal dendrodendritic microcircuits can be found in several parts of the nervous system and are especially abundant in the vertebrate olfactory bulb (Crespo et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Crespo et al., 2013.

claim: In the glomerular layer, the MTC apical tuft is reciprocally connected to mostly periglomerular cell dendrites.
source: In the glomerular layer, the MTC apical tuft is reciprocally connected to mostly periglomerular cell dendrites.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about olfactory bulb circuitry.

claim: In the external plexiform layer, the long MC lateral dendrites are densely covered with GABAergic synapses that mostly originate from reciprocal arrangements.
source: In the external plexiform layer, the long MC lateral dendrites are densely covered with GABAergic synapses that mostly originate from reciprocal arrangements (Bartel et al., 2015; Sailor et al., 2016; Matsuno et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Bartel et al., 2015; Sailor et al., 2016; Matsuno et al., 2017).

claim: Proximal circuits in the external plexiform layer are thought to be mostly formed by granule cell spines.
source: While proximal circuits are thought to be mostly formed by granule cell (GC) spines (Miyamichi et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Miyamichi et al., 2013.

claim: GC spines feature particularly long necks.
source: These spines feature particularly long necks (Woolf et al., 1991)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Woolf et al., 1991.

claim: Long spine necks might serve to electrically isolate the synapse and boost local processing.
source: which might serve to electrically isolate the synapse and boost local processing (e.g. Miller et al., 1985; Spruston, 2008)
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations (Miller et al., 1985; Spruston, 2008).

claim: Unitary postsynaptic potentials in GC spines are electrically compartmentalized.
source: Indeed, we have gathered evidence that unitary postsynaptic potentials in GC spines are electrically compartmentalized and thus can locally activate voltage-gated Na+-channels (Navs)
evidence: This is based on previous work by the authors (Bywalez et al., 2015).

claim: Voltage-gated Na+-channels in GC spines activate classic presynaptic high-voltage-activated Ca2+-channels within the spine.
source: which in turn activate classic presynaptic high-voltage-activated Ca2+-channels (HVACCs) within the spine ('spine spike', Bywalez et al., 2015)
evidence: This is based on previous work by the authors (Bywalez et al., 2015).

claim: The reciprocal spine might operate as a mini-neuron that can generate synaptic output upon local activation.
source: Thus, the reciprocal spine might operate as a mini-neuron that can generate synaptic output upon local activation (Egger and Urban, 2006).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on previous work (Egger and Urban, 2006).

claim: It is unknown whether a unitary, purely local activation of the spine's microcircuit can trigger release of GABA back onto the exciting MTC.
source: it is so far unknown whether a unitary, purely local activation of the spine's microcircuit can indeed trigger release of GABA back onto the exciting MTC
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: TPU of glutamate allows to study the operational mechanisms of the reciprocal microcircuit in single GC spines without causing broader GC activation.
source: TPU of glutamate allows to study the operational mechanisms of the reciprocal microcircuit in single GC spines without causing broader GC activation (Bywalez et al., 2015, see also Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by previous work (Bywalez et al., 2015) and data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Wash-in of 1 mM DNI increased the basal frequency of spontaneous IPSCs by on average 1.9 ± 1.2 times.
source: Wash-in of 1 mM DNI further increased the basal frequency by on average 1.9 ± 1.2 times (mean value before DNI: 4.5 ± 2.1 Hz, n = 14 MCs, p<0.01, Wilcoxon test)
evidence: This is experimental data from the study.

claim: DNI reduced the mean spontaneous IPSC amplitude to a fraction of 0.47 ± 0.16 of control.
source: which also reduced the mean spontaneous IPSC amplitude to a fraction of 0.47 ± 0.16 of control (n = 14 MCs, p<0.001, Wilcoxon test; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B)
evidence: This is experimental data from the study shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Bicuculline (50 µM) blocked spontaneous IPSC activity almost completely in the presence of DNI.
source: In the presence of DNI, the GABAAR antagonist bicuculline (BCC, 50 µM) blocked spontaneous activity almost completely (frequency: 0.13 ± 0.10 of control, n = 6 MCs, p<0.01, Wilcoxon test; Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: MCs were clamped to +10 mV in the main body of experiments, near the reversal potential of ionotropic glutamate receptors.
source: MCs were clamped to +10 mV in the main body of experiments, near the reversal potential of ionotropic glutamate receptors (Isaacson, 1999; Friedman and Strowbridge, 2000)
evidence: This is a methodological choice supported by citations (Isaacson, 1999; Friedman and Strowbridge, 2000).

claim: All experiments were performed at physiological levels of [Mg2+]e (1 mM).
source: All experiments were performed at physiological levels of [Mg2+]e (1 mM).
evidence: This is a methodological detail of the experiments.

claim: Responses were detectable in approximately 30% of tested MCs.
source: Responses were detectable in ∼ 30% of tested MCs (total n = 166 MCs, see Materials and methods)
evidence: This is experimental data from the study.

claim: TPU-evoked signals can be expected to be localized to the stimulated GC spine.
source: In addition, TPU-evoked signals can be expected to be localized to the stimulated GC spine: there is no Ca2+ influx into the adjacent dendritic shaft upon TPU, as we have shown in GC Ca2+ imaging experiments that were performed previously (dye 100 µM OGB-1, average amplitude ratio ∆F/F spine:dendrite 46:2 Bywalez et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by previous Ca2+ imaging data (Bywalez et al., 2015).

claim: There were no detectable Ca2+ transients in non-stimulated spines adjacent to stimulated spines.
source: While the mean amplitude (∆F/F)TPU in the stimulated spine set (∆F/F)TPU = 52 ± 22% was similar to the data set in Bywalez et al., 2015 (p=0.38, Mann-Whitney test), there were no detectable Ca2+ transients in the non-stimulated spines (amplitude 2 ± 2%, p<0.002 vs stimulated spine, Wilcoxon test)
evidence: This is experimental data from the study demonstrating spatial specificity of TPU.

claim: All uncaging spots were located proximally, at distances < 50 µm from the MC soma.
source: All uncaging spots were located proximally, at distances < 50 µm from the MC soma (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is a methodological detail shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Triggered responses were classified as urIPSCs if they were GABAergic.
source: Next, we tested whether these triggered responses were indeed GABAergic by applying the GABAAR antagonist bicuculline (BCC, 50 µM), which invariably blocked responses completely (Figure 1C, n = 7 MCs, p<0.01, Wilcoxon test).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The amplitude of triggered urIPSCs was on average 12 ± 8 pA.
source: The amplitude of triggered urIPSCs was on average 12 ± 8 pA (in n = 32 MCs clamped to +10 mV, Figure 1E)
evidence: This is experimental data from the study shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The amplitude of triggered urIPSCs is significantly smaller than the mean amplitudes of spontaneous IPSCs.
source: which is significantly smaller than the mean amplitudes of spontaneous IPSCs (sIPSCs, n = 14 MCs; 22 ± 12 pA; p<0.001, Mann-Whitney test, Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is experimental data from the study shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The average release probability from the reciprocal spine was estimated as Pr_GABA = 0.34 ± 0.11.
source: The average release probability from the reciprocal spine was estimated as Pr_GABA = 0.34 ± 0.11 (Figure 1E, range 0.13–0.60, based on n = 44 MCs, see Materials and methods and Discussion).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The latencies of urIPSCs were not normally distributed.
source: The latencies of urIPSCs were not normally distributed (Figure 1E), with a first peak within the first 10 ms post TPU onset (n = 13 MCs), a second peak around 30 ms (n = 19 MCs within the range 10–50 ms) and a yet more delayed tail (n = 3 MCs, see Figure 1—figure supplement 1H and Discussion).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Both area and number of events increased highly significantly in the 500 ms interval following TPU compared to the same interval right before.
source: Both area and number of events increased highly significantly in the 500 ms interval following TPU ('post') compared to the same interval right before ('pre'; mean increase of integrated activity ∆_area + 0.50 ± 0.55 relative to 'pre' value; mean increase in event number + 0.25 ± 0.37 relative to 'pre' value; n = 27 MCs, p<0.001 for both, Wilcoxon test
evidence: This is experimental data from the study.

claim: Asynchronous recurrent inhibition can be triggered by single glutamatergic inputs.
source: Thus, asynchronous recurrent inhibition can be already triggered by single glutamatergic inputs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on asynchronous events.

claim: The amplitudes of averaged responses during the first and last 5–10 photostimulations were not significantly different.
source: The amplitudes of averaged responses during the first and last 5–10 photostimulations (with at least 10 min in between to mimic the time course of pharmacological manipulations, mean number of responses per averaged urIPSC 2.8 ± 1.1) were not significantly different (Figure 1F, n = 7 MCs, ratio last to first 0.95 ± 0.15, p=0.74, Wilcoxon test).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study shown in Figure 1F demonstrating stability of recordings.

claim: Local, unitary-like TPU of glutamate can stably trigger both fast and slow reciprocal release of GABA.
source: From all these experiments, we conclude that local, unitary-like TPU of glutamate can stably trigger both fast and slow reciprocal release of GABA, providing proof that the reciprocal microcircuit can be activated by single synaptic inputs at physiological levels of Mg2+.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the section.

claim: Wash-in of TTX (500 nM) substantially reduced both triggered and spontaneous events.
source: Figure 2 illustrates that wash-in of TTX (500 nM) substantially reduced both triggered and spontaneous events.
evidence: This is experimental data from the study shown in Figure 2.

claim: urIPSC amplitudes were reduced to a fraction of 0.17 ± 0.34 of control by TTX.
source: On average, urIPSC amplitudes were reduced to a fraction of 0.17 ± 0.34 of control (Figure 2D, n = 12 MCs, p<0.005, Cohen's d = 2.54, Wilcoxon test
evidence: This is experimental data from the study shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The frequency of spontaneous activity was strongly decreased in TTX, to a fraction of 0.24 ± 0.17 of control.
source: While the frequency of spontaneous activity was also strongly decreased in TTX, to a fraction of 0.24 ± 0.17 of control (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, n = 10 MCs, p<0.005)
evidence: This is experimental data from the study shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The mean sIPSC amplitude was unchanged by TTX.
source: the mean sIPSC amplitude was unchanged by TTX (1.36 ± 0.68 of control, n.s., n = 10 MCs, Figure 2A,B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B)
evidence: This is experimental data from the study shown in Figure 2A,B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Navs are essential to trigger GABA release from the reciprocal spines.
source: Thus Navs are essential to trigger GABA release from the reciprocal spines.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the TTX experiments.

claim: Blockade of NPQ-type Ca2+ channels with 1 µM ω-conotoxin MVIIC resulted in a substantial decrease of urIPSCs, to a fraction of 0.08 ± 0.14 of control.
source: Figure 3 shows the resulting substantial decrease of urIPSCs, to a fraction of 0.08 ± 0.14 of control (from a mean amplitude of 11.3 ± 5.7 pA; n = 8 MCs, p<0.005, Cohen's d = 6.6, Figure 3D).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study shown in Figure 3.

claim: CTX decreased sIPSC frequency to a fraction of 0.53 ± 0.15 of control, less markedly than TTX.
source: CTX decreased sIPSC frequency to a fraction of 0.53 ± 0.15 of control, less markedly than TTX (Figure 3E, n = 7 MCs, control vs CTX: p<0.01; CTX vs TTX: p<0.005; Mann-Whitney test)
evidence: This is experimental data from the study shown in Figure 3E.

claim: HVACC activation is required for release of GABA from the reciprocal spine following local input.
source: We conclude that HVACC activation is also required for release of GABA from the reciprocal spine following local input.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the CTX experiments.

claim: Application of 25 µM D-APV resulted in a substantial decrease of urIPSC amplitudes, to on average 0.22 ± 0.21 of control.
source: Figure 4A–D shows that the application of 25 µM D-APV resulted in a substantial decrease of urIPSC amplitudes, to on average 0.22 ± 0.21 of control (from a mean amplitude of 13.8 ± 8.6 pA, n = 10 MCs, p<0.002, Cohen's d = 3.7, Wilcoxon test; Figure 4D).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study shown in Figure 4A–D.

claim: APV substantially reduced sIPSC frequency, to 0.27 ± 0.23 of control.
source: While APV also substantially reduced sIPSC frequency, to 0.27 ± 0.23 of control (n = 10 MCs, p<0.005, Figure 4A,B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B), similar to TTX (p=0.79) and significantly more pronounced than CTX (p<0.01)
evidence: This is experimental data from the study shown in Figure 4A,B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: APV application significantly reduced the mean AHP amplitude to a fraction of 0.86 ± 0.11 of control.
source: Figure 4F shows that APV application significantly reduced the mean AHP amplitude to a fraction of 0.86 ± 0.11 of control (p<0.0001, Wilcoxon test, Cohen's d = 0.86; reduction in 17 of 18 MCs)
evidence: This is experimental data from the study shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Occlusion experiments using APV before GBZ or GBZ before APV did not result in any further reduction of AHP amplitude.
source: Occlusion experiments using APV before GBZ or GBZ before APV did not result in any further reduction (0.97 ± 0.09 of amplitude in the presence of first drug, n = 12 MCs, p=0.16, Wilcoxon test, Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: NMDARs located on GCs are strongly involved in reciprocal release.
source: From these and the uncaging experiments we conclude that NMDARs located on GCs are strongly involved in reciprocal release, even though prevention of HVACC activation (via Nav block or pharmacology) also blocks reciprocal release.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the APV experiments and AHP experiments.

claim: The local AP causes a transient boosting of the NMDAR Ca2+ current because of further relief of the Mg2+ block during the upstroke and overshoot of the spine spike.
source: Figure 5A shows a simulation of the postsynaptic NMDAR- and HVACC-mediated Ca2+ currents (based on the detailed NEURON model described in Aghvami et al., 2019, see Materials and methods) which illustrates that the local AP causes a transient boosting of the NMDAR Ca2+ current because of further relief of the Mg2+ block during the upstroke and overshoot of the spine spike.
evidence: This is demonstrated through computational modeling shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The fast NMDAR-mediated Ca2+ spikelet begins even before the HVACC-mediated current and tightly overlaps with it within >1 ms.
source: According to the simulation this fast NMDAR-mediated Ca2+ spikelet begins even before the HVACC-mediated current and tightly overlaps with it within >1 ms.
evidence: This is demonstrated through computational modeling shown in Figure 5A.

claim: When both symmetric and asymmetric synaptic profiles were visible in individual GC-MC dendrodendritic pairs, the two synaptic profiles were mostly either contiguous (44% of n = 60 cases) or closer than 100 nm (36% of cases).
source: Interestingly, we observed that when both symmetric and asymmetric synaptic profiles were visible in individual GC-MC dendrodendritic pairs, the two synaptic profiles were mostly either contiguous (44% of n = 60 cases, examples Figure 6A2, A3, cumulative plot Figure 6B) or closer than 100 nm (36% of cases).
evidence: This is ultrastructural data from the study shown in Figure 6.

claim: Immunogold labeling for NMDARs was frequently observed in symmetric contacts.
source: Immunogold labeling for NMDARs was also frequently observed in symmetric contacts, albeit at a lesser density compared to asymmetric contacts (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is ultrastructural data from the study shown in Figure 6A.

claim: For GluN1, there were 50 particles along 84.5 µm of 138 non-synaptic spine membrane segments (mean 0.6 particles/µm).
source: For GluN1, there were 50 particles along 84.5 µm of 138 non-synaptic spine membrane segments (mean 0.6 particles/µm)
evidence: This is ultrastructural data from the study.

claim: For GluN1, there were 70 particles along 32.7 µm of 120 symmetric profiles (mean 2.1 particles/µm).
source: 70 particles along 32.7 µm of 120 symmetric profiles (mean 2.1 particles/µm)
evidence: This is ultrastructural data from the study.

claim: For GluN1, there were 394 particles along 28.6 µm of 111 asymmetric profiles (mean 13.8 particles/µm).
source: 394 particles along 28.6 µm of 111 asymmetric profiles (mean 13.8 particles/µm)
evidence: This is ultrastructural data from the study.

claim: The distribution of the density of gold particles at symmetric synapses was significantly higher than the one in non-synaptic membrane for GluN1.
source: The distribution of the density of gold particles at symmetric synapses was significantly higher than the one in non-synaptic membrane (p=0.000029, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test).
evidence: This is ultrastructural data from the study with statistical analysis.

claim: For GluN2A/B, the density distribution at symmetric synapses was significantly higher than the distribution at the non-synaptic membrane.
source: Still, the density distribution at symmetric synapses was significantly higher than the distribution at the non-synaptic membrane (p=0.000048).
evidence: This is ultrastructural data from the study with statistical analysis.

claim: Labeling of symmetric synapses was considerably stronger for GluN2A/B vs GluN1.
source: Interestingly, while the labeling densities for GluN1 and GluN2A/B were similar across non-synaptic membranes and asymmetric synapses each (p=0.99 and p=0.81, respectively), labeling of symmetric synapses was considerably stronger for GluN2A/B vs GluN1 (p=0.00042).
evidence: This is ultrastructural data from the study with statistical analysis.

claim: The distribution of both GluN1 and GluN2A/B label at asymmetric synapses was similar, with a main peak just inside the postsynaptic GC membrane and another peak within the synaptic cleft.
source: The distribution of both GluN1 and GluN2A/B label at asymmetric synapses was similar, with a main peak just inside the postsynaptic GC membrane and another peak within the synaptic cleft.
evidence: This is ultrastructural data from the study analyzing radial distribution.

claim: The distribution of gold particles at symmetric synapses mirrored the one at asymmetric synapses, implying that labeling for NMDARs is predominantly associated with both the presynaptic GABAergic and the postsynaptic glutamatergic membrane of GCs.
source: Notably, the distribution of gold particles at symmetric synapses mirrored the one at asymmetric synapses, implying that labeling for NMDARs is predominantly associated with both the presynaptic GABAergic and the postsynaptic glutamatergic membrane of GCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ultrastructural data analyzing radial distribution.

claim: NMDARs play a direct presynaptic role for GABA release from the reciprocal spine, albeit in cooperation with the spine spike.
source: In summary, we conclude from the combined physiological, computational and ultrastructural evidence that NMDARs do play a direct presynaptic role for GABA release from the reciprocal spine, albeit in cooperation with the spine spike
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental and computational evidence.

claim: The cooperation between NMDARs and HVACCs could be mediated by overlapping NMDAR- and HVACC-mediated Ca2+ entry.
source: and propose that this cooperation could be mediated by overlapping NMDAR- and HVACC-mediated Ca2+ entry (Figure 7)
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the experimental and computational evidence, illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: Any inhibitory output from a GC spine will require the presence of glutamate and thus synaptic input to the respective spine.
source: A direct consequence of this conclusion is that any inhibitory output from a GC spine will require the presence of glutamate and thus synaptic input to the respective spine (except perhaps for GC action potential bursts)
evidence: This is a logical inference from the finding that NMDARs are required for GABA release.

claim: Under physiological conditions close to the MC resting potential, the size of the fast IPSCs is on the order of −5 pA.
source: For the proximal reciprocal GC inputs investigated here we estimate that under physiological conditions close to the MC resting potential the size of the fast IPSCs is on the order of −5 pA, after corrections for the partial GABAAR block by DNI and the setting of ECl.
evidence: This is an estimate based on experimental data with corrections applied.

claim: An inhibitory input from a single GC spine will exert a somatic hyperpolarization of at best 0.5 mV.
source: Thus, assuming an in vivo MC input resistance of 100 MΩ (Angelo and Margrie, 2011), an inhibitory input from a single GC spine will exert a somatic hyperpolarization of at best 0.5 mV
evidence: This is a calculation based on experimental data and cited in vivo measurements (Angelo and Margrie, 2011).

claim: Even proximal GC inputs will barely influence MC firing unless there is coordinated activity across GC spines connected to the same MC dendrite.
source: and therefore even proximal GC inputs will barely influence MC firing (Fukunaga et al., 2014; McIntyre and Cleland, 2016) - unless there is coordinated activity across GC spines connected to the same MC dendrite
evidence: This is an inference based on the calculated small amplitude and supported by citations (Fukunaga et al., 2014; McIntyre and Cleland, 2016).

claim: The observed Pr_GABA might represent an upper limit because the global reduction of inhibition by DNI could cause a homeostatic upregulation of Pr_GABA.
source: This value might represent an upper limit, because the global reduction of inhibition by DNI could cause a homeostatic upregulation of Pr_GABA (e.g. Rannals and Kapur, 2011)
evidence: This is speculation about potential confounding factors, supported by citation (Rannals and Kapur, 2011).

claim: Pr_GABA might become further downregulated during development, since recurrent inhibition was shown to decrease in older animals.
source: Moreover, Pr_GABA might become further downregulated during development, since recurrent inhibition was shown to decrease in older animals (Dietz et al., 2011; Duménieu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations (Dietz et al., 2011; Duménieu et al., 2015).

claim: The efficiency of the entire reciprocal microcircuit can be estimated as Preciprocal = Pr_Glu • Pr_GABA ≈ 0.2.
source: With Pr_GABA ≈ 0.3 and the probability for MC glutamate release on the order of Pr_Glu ≈ 0.5–0.75 (Egger et al., 2005; Pressler and Strowbridge, 2017) the efficiency of the entire reciprocal microcircuit can be estimated as Preciprocal = Pr_Glu • Pr_GABA ≈ 0.2
evidence: This is a calculation based on experimental data and cited values (Egger et al., 2005; Pressler and Strowbridge, 2017).

claim: GC spines are likely to release with higher probabilities upon coincident non-local GC signaling due to substantially increased ΔCa2+ in the spine.
source: The rather low Pr_GABA observed here also implies that GC spines are likely to release with higher probabilities upon coincident non-local GC signaling (i.e. regional or global Ca2+ or Na+ spikes), due to substantially increased ∆Ca2+ in the spine as observed previously (Egger et al., 2005; Egger, 2008; Aghvami et al., 2019; Mueller and Egger, 2020).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed low Pr_GABA and supported by citations (Egger et al., 2005; Egger, 2008; Aghvami et al., 2019; Mueller and Egger, 2020).

claim: The fastest urIPSCs were detected within 2 ms from TPU onset.
source: Figure 1E shows that the fastest urIPSCs were detected within 2 ms from TPU onset
evidence: This is experimental data from the study shown in Figure 1E.

claim: There is a fast mechanism coupling Ca2+ entry to release at the GC spine.
source: implying that there is a fast mechanism coupling Ca2+ entry to release - in line with earlier findings of tight coupling between Ca2+ entry and GABA release (using EGTA, Isaacson, 2001), and of a crucial role for Nav channels (Bywalez et al., 2015; Nunes and Kuner, 2018)
evidence: This is an inference from the latency data, supported by citations (Isaacson, 2001; Bywalez et al., 2015; Nunes and Kuner, 2018).

claim: Substantial asynchronous release from the GC spine on longer time scales (detected at up to 500 ms post TPU) was frequently observed.
source: In any case, substantial asynchronous release from the GC spine on yet longer time scales (detected at up to 500 ms post TPU) was frequently observed, in line with earlier studies on recurrent inhibition that localized the origin of asynchronous signaling within GCs (Schoppa et al., 1998; Chen et al., 2000; Isaacson, 2001).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study, supported by citations (Schoppa et al., 1998; Chen et al., 2000; Isaacson, 2001).

claim: Ca2+ entry via NMDARs occurs independently from Ca2+ entry mediated by the Nav-HVACC pathway.
source: Previously we had shown via occlusion experiments that Ca2+ entry via NMDARs occurs independently from Ca2+ entry mediated by the Nav-HVACC pathway, since AMPAR-mediated depolarization on its own is strong enough to lift the Mg2+ block, probably due to boosting by the high GC spine neck resistance (Bywalez et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on previous work by the authors (Bywalez et al., 2015).

claim: TPU resulted in a slightly larger NMDA-receptor-mediated component of the postsynaptic Ca2+ signal than true synaptic activation via glomerular stimulation.
source: We had observed that TPU resulted in a slightly larger NMDA-receptor-mediated component of the postsynaptic Ca2+ signal than true synaptic activation via glomerular stimulation (~65% vs ~50% of ∆F/F Bywalez et al., 2015; Egger et al., 2005).
evidence: This is based on previous work by the authors (Bywalez et al., 2015; Egger et al., 2005).

claim: NMDAR blockade alone does not prevent GC spine spike generation.
source: Therefore, we investigated recurrent inhibition elicited by single MC APs, and could demonstrate that NMDAR blockade alone (which does not prevent GC spine spike generation, Bywalez et al., 2015) also reduces recurrent inhibition.
evidence: This is experimental data from the study, with reference to previous work (Bywalez et al., 2015).

claim: PV+ cells feature Ca2+-permeable AMPARs and a probably absent NMDAR component in response to MTC input.
source: Another interesting aspect of the strong influence of NMDARs on GC output is that this property might serve to differentiate the MC↔GC microcircuit from the MC↔PV+ cell microcircuit, since PV+ cells feature Ca2+-permeable AMPARs and a probably absent NMDAR component in response to MTC input (Kato et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation (Kato et al., 2013).

claim: In the earlier study of TPU-evoked Ca2+ signals in GC spines, there was no obvious influence of Nav activation on NMDAR-mediated Ca2+ entry.
source: In our earlier study of TPU-evoked Ca2+ signals in GC spines there was no obvious influence of Nav activation on NMDAR-mediated Ca2+ entry (Bywalez et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on previous work by the authors (Bywalez et al., 2015).

claim: The simulations indicate that the extra contribution of Nav-mediated boosting of NMDAR Ca2+ current is not substantial in terms of added ΔF/F under experimental conditions.
source: However, the simulations also indicate that this extra contribution is not substantial in terms of added ∆F/F under our experimental conditions and therefore could not be detected (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through computational modeling shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The earlier the postsynaptic membrane is depolarized after glutamate release, the more efficiently NMDARs will be activated.
source: In line with the fast NMDAR-mediated Ca2+ spikelet, Kampa et al., 2004 have shown that the earlier the postsynaptic membrane is depolarized after glutamate release, the more efficiently NMDARs will be activated.
evidence: This is supported by citation (Kampa et al., 2004).

claim: Presynaptic actions of NMDARs at specific subsets of both glutamatergic and GABAergic synapses have recently received attention.
source: Presynaptic actions of NMDARs at specific subsets of both glutamatergic and GABAergic synapses have recently received attention (reviewed in Bouvier et al., 2015; Banerjee et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles (Bouvier et al., 2015; Banerjee et al., 2016).

claim: Presynaptic NMDARs have been shown to play a role in plasticity induction.
source: Presynaptic NMDARs have been shown to play a role in plasticity induction (e.g. Duguid and Smart, 2004)
evidence: This is supported by citation (Duguid and Smart, 2004).

claim: Presynaptic NMDARs are involved in modulation of basal synaptic transmission, where effects are mostly observed upon repetitive transmitter release.
source: or in modulation of basal synaptic transmission, where effects are mostly observed upon repetitive transmitter release (e.g. McGuinness et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citation (McGuinness et al., 2010).

claim: In the cerebellum, presynaptic NMDARs are involved in enhancing spontaneous release of GABA.
source: In the cerebellum, presynaptic NMDARs are also involved in enhancing spontaneous release of GABA (Glitsch and Marty, 1999)
evidence: This is supported by citation (Glitsch and Marty, 1999).

claim: Direct triggering of release via presynaptic NMDARs during unitary transmission has not been observed before this study.
source: However, to our knowledge direct triggering of release via presynaptic NMDARs during unitary transmission has not been observed so far
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings based on knowledge of the literature.

claim: Spontaneous IPSCs are likely to predominantly originate from the more proximal lateral MC dendrites.
source: Spontaneous IPSCs are likely to predominantly originate from the more proximal lateral MC dendrites (Arnson and Strowbridge, 2017).

claim: Nav blockade was shown to strongly reduce MC sIPSC frequencies but not amplitude.
source: Nav blockade was already shown to strongly reduce MC sIPSC frequencies but not amplitude (e.g. Saghatelyan et al., 2005; Arnson and Strowbridge, 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations (Saghatelyan et al., 2005; Arnson and Strowbridge, 2017).

claim: A substantial effect of NMDAR blockade on sIPSC frequencies was observed in other olfactory bulb studies.
source: A substantial effect of NMDAR blockade on sIPSC frequencies was also observed in other olfactory bulb studies (Wellis and Kauer, 1993; Schmidt and Strowbridge, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Wellis and Kauer, 1993; Schmidt and Strowbridge, 2014).

claim: There is substantial prior evidence for both the activity-dependence and NMDAR-dependence of GC-mediated lateral inhibition.
source: There is substantial prior evidence in the literature for both the activity-dependence and NMDAR-dependence of GC-mediated lateral inhibition (Arevian et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation (Arevian et al., 2008).

claim: NMDAR blockade is routinely used to dissect lateral inhibition in the glomerular layer from GC-mediated lateral inhibition.
source: NMDAR blockade is routinely used to dissect lateral inhibition in the glomerular layer from GC-mediated lateral inhibition (Shao et al., 2012; Najac et al., 2015; Geramita and Urban, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Shao et al., 2012; Najac et al., 2015; Geramita and Urban, 2017).

claim: In in vivo MC recordings, there was a subset of MCs that responded exclusively with inhibition to odor activation, mediated via glomerular layer neurons but not via GCs.
source: Yet more importantly, in in vivo MC recordings there was a subset of MCs that responded exclusively with inhibition to odor activation, mediated via glomerular layer neurons but not via GCs (Fukunaga et al., 2014, their Figures 4 and 7).
evidence: This is supported by citation (Fukunaga et al., 2014).

claim: Both GC NMDARs and Navs play a role specifically in discriminations between binary odorant mixtures in mice.
source: As to behavioral evidence for our hypothesis, both GC NMDARs and Navs are known to play a role specifically in discriminations between binary odorant mixtures in mice, since in the same behavioral paradigm GC-specific knock-down (in about ~50% of GCs) of the NMDAR-subunit GluN1 resulted in an increase in discrimination time of on average ~60 ms, and knock-down of Navs of ~85 ms vs control, while discriminations between pure odors were not affected (Abraham et al., 2010; Nunes and Kuner, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Abraham et al., 2010; Nunes and Kuner, 2018).

claim: Reciprocal spines allow the GC to selectively interact with coactive glomerular columns.
source: In summary, our findings suggest that reciprocal spines allow the GC to selectively interact with coactive glomerular columns.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the findings of the study.

claim: The reciprocal spine might be a circuit motif that specifically enables efficient binding of dispersed olfactory representations.
source: Thus, the reciprocal spine might be a circuit motif that specifically enables efficient binding of dispersed olfactory representations, a coding task that this sensory modality needs to perform due to its large number of receptors.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the findings of the study.

claim: Reciprocal spines with their unique synaptic arrangement and functionality are likely to represent a special adaptation to the demands of sensory processing in the bulb.
source: In other words, reciprocal spines with their unique synaptic arrangement and functionality, including spine spikes and presynaptic NMDARs, are likely to represent a special adaptation to the demands of sensory processing in the bulb.
